en: In that regard, on an auspicious day, preceded by the offering of a bali-oblation, the ground for the monastery and so forth should be thoroughly examined.
On an auspicious day, preceded by the offering of a bali-oblation, the ground for the monastery and so forth should be thoroughly examined.

In that regard, the earth— possessing white, red, yellow, and black appearances, and having the odors of semen, blood, urine, and excrement, and possessing sweet, astringent, sour, and pungent tastes—
belongs respectively to the Brahmins and the other castes.
The earth is white and bestows fruit in pacification; it is red-hued in subjugation; the two following that [in attraction and expulsion] are yellow and black respectively;
and its color is never otherwise than yellow in nourishment or black in ferocity.
[Is it] not another noble [mantra]?

From the white ground, one bestows the fruit of peace; from the red color, one performs subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Beyond that, the latter two grounds—those of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*) and wrath (*abhicāruka*)—arise from the yellow and the black-white colors, and not from any other.

The eight floating islands of the earth, starting from the east and proceeding in order, are known to bring about success in liberation from the fears of old age, disease, death, grief, and loss of wealth.
O noble lady, prosperity, illness,
death, sorrow, loss of wealth, fear, liberation, and accomplishment— these eight should be understood as occurring respectively in the east and the other directions from the ground of inclination.
Although land purified by a flood is said to bring about auspiciousness,
it would be even more highly beneficial if it flows toward the northeast.
If it is explained that ground sloping toward the east or north makes for virtue, then ground sloping toward the east and north from that [location] will be even more excellent.
A ground covered with anthills causes disease; one that is parched leads to the loss of wealth; one that is cracked brings death;
and one with fruitless tips is the lowest of all; such uneven ground produces misfortune.

From the presence of a fortress of gravel comes internal strife; from harsh ground, the depletion of wealth; from cracked ground, the absence of excellent fruit; and from low-lying ground, lightness and undesirable things.
One should avoid ground that is bow-shaped, triangular, circular, or crooked;
likewise, ground characterized by features such as the back of a tortoise must be avoided.
One should avoid those that have the shape of a bow, are triangular, contain water, or are curved; one should also avoid those characterized by features such as the back of a tortoise.
Furthermore:
one should avoid the Aśvattha tree in the east, likewise the Arjuna in the southeast,
the Plakṣa in the southern direction, and the Palāśa born from a Jātudhāna (demon).
"One should avoid the *nyagrodha* tree in the western part, the *śālmalī* in the north-west, the *bakula* in the north, and the *udumbara* in the north-east. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, Padmaśrīmitra says: "Moreover, one should avoid Aśvattha in the east, and likewise Ārdhana in the southeast; Plakṣa in the southern direction, and Palāśa in the southwest; Nyagrodha in the western direction, and Śālmalī in the northwest; Bakula in the northern direction, and Audumbara in the northeast."
Thereafter,
having dug a pit one span deep and quickly filling it with that soil,
if the soil should be in excess, then it brings about auspiciousness.
If it should be deficient, however, it must be abandoned by those who perceive its faults.

Then, having dug to the depth of one span, he should quickly fill it with that same earth. If that earth remains in excess, it is a sign of auspiciousness; if it becomes deficient, knowing it to be defective, he should abandon it.
Then, having taken earth from that pit, one should fill it with water to the depth of a span.
Having gone a full hundred steps and returned again, the practitioner of mantra should examine the ground; he should avoid a site that is empty, even if it appears auspicious and filled with water.

Having filled [the vessel] and walked one hundred paces, one should return once more and examine it. Where the water remains full, that ground is excellent; where it has subsided, the practitioner of mantras should avoid it.
If the water here makes a sound, one should predict fear from the *nāgas*;
thereafter, having grasped it auspiciously, one should proceed according to the rite prescribed by rule.
If that water were accompanied by sound, it would truly manifest fear among the nāgas.
Having subsequently seen the ritual, those of virtuous karma shall be fully embraced.

Thus, the teacher—who has understood the characteristics of the site, has bathed, is pure, has his limbs scented with fragrance, has prepared the requisites for worship, has dressed himself in whatever garments and ornaments he obtained, and has well-cultivated the yoga of the deity—at the time of evening, in the center of that site, upon a ground smeared to the extent of four cubits in a square, having fashioned a mandala there with cow dung and other materials, having meditated upon the wheel of the mandala therein and worshipped it, and having offered the bali-oblation to the directions, places his right knee-knot upon the earth while wearing his upper garment.
With palms joined, one should request the earth from the fully awakened ones, bodhisattvas, world-protectors, and others stationed in the cardinal and intermediate directions.

Thus, the master who knows the characteristics of the earth, having bathed and anointed his pure body with fragrant scents, having properly arranged the articles of worship, and having dressed himself in whatever robes and ornaments are available, should practice the yoga of the deity thoroughly.
On that ground, which is four cubits in measure and square in shape, one should perform the ritual preparation by means of [the syllable] *ba* and so forth.

Having meditated upon the mandala circle, having made perfect offerings and given the directional *bali* offerings, one should kneel with the right knee on the ground, arrange the upper robe over one shoulder, join the palms together, and receive [the empowerment] from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas residing in the cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as from the World Protectors and others.
To those lords who dwell in this triple world, the most magnificent—
the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and so forth—
I address them all for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of every sentient being.
On this beautiful stretch of land, for the sake of the flourishing of monasteries,
and for the realization of the true nature of reality (dharmatā) through the noble conduct of hearing, reflection,
and so forth, I, [Name], am intent upon establishing the excellent fame of [Name].
If it pleases you, I shall act otherwise; indeed, not otherwise.
By means of signs such as dreams and the like, you shall grant me this auspicious earth.
Wherever in the three realms the Protectors reside, being honored by the Great One—
Gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, and so forth—
I pray for this to each of them, in order to accomplish the welfare of all sentient beings.
Having erected a temple here with its excellent parts, he...
Because you abide in the supreme [practices] such as hearing and reflection, in order to realize the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā),...
"I am so-and-so; I strive to bring about excellent renown."
If you grant me your forgiveness, I shall do it; otherwise, I will not.
"By means of signs such as dreams and so forth, please bestow upon me this excellent stage."
Thus one should recite three times.
Thus it should be recited three times.

Thereafter, having consecrated his face twenty-one times with the left hand using this *svapnamāṇavaka* mantra—namely, *oṃ mucili svāhā*, *oṃ mohami svāhā*, *oṃ dattili svāhā*—he should lie down in a pure place with his head toward the south and facing east, adorned with clean ornaments, having first performed worship before the Blessed One Lokeśvara, and sleep as he pleases.

Regarding bad dreams, however, one should perform what is described below either by reciting the Amṛtakuṇḍalin mantra or by resolving upon the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena; provided that, on a site either granted or not prohibited by the deities, one has fashioned a young boy (*māṇavaka*) representing the dream. But if the site is prohibited, one should certainly not do so.

Following that, with this dream-examination mantra: *oṃ mucili svāhā | oṃ mohani svāhā | oṃ dittali svāhā*, one should recite it twenty-one times over the fingers of the left hand. Then, preceded by an offering before the Blessed One Lokeśvara, having adorned oneself with clean garments, facing east with the head pointing south, as follows:

One should go to sleep with desire; if the dream is bad, one should recite the Amṛtakuṇḍalī mantra or resolve that all phenomena are ultimately without intrinsic nature. Having examined the dream once more, one should perform the practices explained below on a site either authorized or not prohibited by the deities; however, one must certainly not do so on a site that has been prohibited.

On the second auspicious day, during a good dream, in the forenoon, seated in the vajraparyaṅka posture and possessing the yoga of Vajrasattva, one should contemplate emptiness with the mantra *oṃ bhūḥ kham*, and then [contemplate] the earth as consisting of vajra-paramāṇus with *hūṃ laṃ hūṃ*. One should then consecrate it with the vajrabandha mudrā, reciting: *oṃ medini vajrībhava vajrabandha hūṃ*.

If the dream is auspicious, on a second auspicious day, during the morning time, one should assume the earth-pressing mudrā and the vajra-paryaṅka posture. Possessing the yoga of Vajrasattva, one should meditate on emptiness with the mantra *oṃ bhūkhaṃ* and on the nature of vajra-atomic particles with the mantra *hūṃ laṃ hūṃ*.
Reciting "oṃ me di nī vajrabhava vajrabandha hūṃ," one should perform the consecration with the vajra-terrifying mudrā.

Having uttered three *hūṃ*s with the index finger of the right hand, and by means of the rays [emitted] from those [syllables], the touching of the tips of the fingers, and their sounds, one should stimulate the Earth-deity from the ground; she emerges either with half her body or her entire body, holding a golden vase in one hand and making the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) with the other, and being well-adorned. One should then worship her with flowers and other offerings, preceded by water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), and the respectful offering (*argha*).

Visualizing a moon disc with the syllable *hūṃ* upon the right hand, one recites [the mantra] three times. By striking [the earth] with its light rays and the tips of the fingers, she is exhorted by those sounds; thereupon, the yellow Earth Goddess emerges, either half-bodied or in her entirety, holding a golden vase and the mudrā of fearlessness in her two hands, adorned with beautiful ornaments, and [one offers] water for washing the feet.
Having made perfect offerings with water for rinsing the mouth and the arghya, preceded by flowers and so forth,
[one recites]: "O Goddess, you are the witness of all the Buddhas, the Protectors,
regarding the specificities of the conduct-vehicle and the stages and perfections."

Just as the army of Māra was defeated by the Protector, the Lion of the Śākyas, so too, having conquered the army of Māra, I shall construct monasteries and other edifices. O Goddess, you have attained mastery over the conduct, the specific qualities, the stages, and the perfections of all the Protectors, the Buddhas. Just as the Protector, the Lion of the Śākyas, vanquished the hosts of Māra, so shall I, having conquered them, build temples and the like.
Thus, when she has been requested three times, one should contemplate her as having said, "Let it be done so," and then as having vanished right there, established in the form of the earth.
Having thus supplicated three times, [the deity] replied, "Do so," and dissolved right there; one should then visualize that the Earth Goddess remains in the form of the earth.
Then, on that ground, one should visualize a peaked pavilion produced from the syllable *bhrūṃ* and a wheel produced from the syllable *bhrūṃ*.

Then, having prepared a fragrance mandala within the interior of the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*), one should summon the wisdom mandala and the guardians of the directions with rays from the seed-syllable in one's own heart; preceded by the offering of water for the feet and other honors, as well as the ritual oblation (*bali*), one—whose tongue is a vajra born from *hūṃ*—holding an incense burner and ringing a bell, [should proceed].

Then, having prepared a fragrance maṇḍala within the tiered pavilion, one should invite the wisdom maṇḍala and the directional deities, such as the *lokapālas*, with light rays from the seed-syllable at one’s own heart. Preceded by offerings such as water for the feet and the presentation of the *bali* offering, one transforms the tongue into a vajra from the syllable *hūṃ*. Holding the incense burner and ringing the bell, one recites:
*Bhagavan amukasad-vajra vidyārāja namo ’stu te.*

O Compassionate One, O Blessed One, Great Vajra Supreme, King of Vidya, I bow to you; I desire to properly offer you the water of honor (argha). O You whose very nature is perfect compassion, I wish to present this offering to you.
Out of compassion for the disciples, for your own worship,
for the sake of increasing the merit of sentient beings, and for the arising of the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
Therefore, O Blessed One, you ought to grant your grace to me, your devotee.
May the Buddhas, who strive for the welfare of the world’s cycle of activity,
turn their attention toward me.
The Bodhisattvas established in the fruit, and those other mantra-deities,
the gods and world-protectors,
and the spirits who are steadfast in awakening;
"O beings who delight in the teaching, and you others who possess the divine eye:
I am such-and-such, the Great Vajrin; I shall now perform the water-offering for such-and-such [deity]. Therefore, you ought to remain present."

May those beings who delight in the Teaching, and others who possess the divine eye, please turn their attention toward me. I, [Name], the great Vajra-holder, am performing this offering to [Name]; therefore, it is fitting that you all remain present.
One should recite it three times.
Thus it should be recited three times.

Then, having placed the victory-vases and others to be described—alternatively, other vases containing live fish inside—in due order, and having performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*), one should fashion the ritual assistants in the forms of deities such as Vighnāntaka who perform all rites; with them, one should dig a square pit two cubits wide at the top and one cubit deep at the bottom.

Then, having placed the victory vase (*vijaya-kalaśa*) and so forth—which will be described later—or, in their absence, other vases containing living fish, one should arrange them in sequence and perform the ritual of consecration (*adhivāsana*). The officiants, manifesting as the deities of all-acting rites such as Vighnāntaka and others, should dig a square pit two cubits wide and one cubit deep.
And to its northeast,
there is a circle of that same measurement or half of it.

Having smeared both of those with clay and cow dung, one should then take white flowers together with *durvā* grass from a square pit using the tips of the index finger and thumb as if with tongs; having whirled them playfully while releasing the index, middle, ring, and little fingers in succession, one should offer the *argha* with the mantra: "Oṃ āḥ, accept this most excellent *argha* of honor, hūṃ svāhā," and then [offer it again] with the mantra: "Oṃ bhrūṃ haḥ hrīḥ, accept [this], bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā."

One should offer water from the victory-pitcher and the other pitchers in their proper order; and just as one fills a square [vessel] completely, so should one fill a circular one by means of a stream.

Both of those should be smeared with earth and cow dung. Then, from the vessel of the *argha* offering, one should take a white flower together with its stalk at the center of a square pit, using the tips of the index finger and the thumb; while circling it completely, one should gradually release the index, middle, ring, and little fingers in the manner of a graceful arch.

Having offered the water for the feet with the mantra: *oṃ āḥ hrīḥ pravarasatkāra arghaṃ pratīccha hūṃ svāhā*, one should fill the square [mandala] exactly as it is by pouring the water from the *vijaya* (victory) vase and other vases in succession with the mantra: *oṃ bhrūṃ haḥ hrīḥ pratīccha bhuvā svāḥ*. Then, one should fill the circle using that same stream.

Thereafter, having observed water swirling to the right and containing cool living fish, and having offered a sprig from a milky tree, one should visualize oneself in the form of Jāṅgulī: yellow in color, with three faces—the central, right, and left—yellow, black, and white respectively; possessing seven hoods and a jeweled crown; six-armed, holding a vajra and an arrow in her two right hands, and a bow and a noose with a threatening gesture (tarjanī) in her two left hands; embraced by her own consort as the means (upāya); adorned with variegated garments and nāga ornaments on the remaining arms; seated upon a sun-disc on a universal lotus, and radiant with light. This is the form of Jāṅgulī.

Visualizing oneself in fivefold form, having performed the *kamalāvarta* [mudrā], and having visualized the earth as consisting of universal vajras by looking down as far as the netherworld (*rasātala*), one should worship the spectators with betel, garlands, and sandalwood.

Following that, having placed a raw fish and a live fish [into the vessel], one should visualize them swirling to the right; then, having inserted leaves of a milky tree, one visualizes oneself as born from the syllable *jaṃ* as Vajra, and from the syllable *jaṃ* as a yellow *jāṅgulī*, with three faces—yellow, black, and white—possessing seven hoods and a jeweled crown, with six arms, the right...

With her two right hands she holds a vajra and an arrow, and with her left hands she holds a bow and a noose together with the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*). With her remaining hands she embraces her consort, who is her own radiance. She is adorned with various garments and snakes, and sits upon a seat of a multicolored lotus and the sun.

Visualize [the site] as having the radiance of the sun; perform the lotus-circle five times and, by contemplating it as culminating in the great empowerment (*mahābhiṣeka*), consider the ground to be of the nature of the variegated vajra (*viśvavajra*). One should also fully satisfy the worldly spectators with tooth-sticks, flower garlands, sandalwood, and so forth.
Thus ends the ritual for examining the ground for the purpose of constructing a monastery and the like. (2)
This is the ritual for thoroughly examining the ground for the purpose of constructing temples and other such edifices.
